opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a really interesting possibility, and it's one of the big differences between digital intelligences and people. A person can't make copies of themselves. If I want to learn about something, I have to go do it myself, and I have only one lifetime. A digital mind with more computation could spawn a copy, send it off to learn about some particular part of the world, have it gain a lot of experience, and then bring that knowledge back.

But I think the hard part, the part people don't appreciate, is the reporting back. How do you merge what that copy learned into the original? Making a copy is easy. Integrating knowledge is not. You can't just paste a big chunk of weights or experience into a mind and expect it to fit. It has to be reconciled with everything else the mind already knows. That's an unsolved problem, and it connects to continual learning, which our methods are still bad at. Our networks tend to forget catastrophically, or they lose plasticity and stop learning well. So the infrastructure for this kind of cooperative learning just isn't there yet.

There's also a danger. If you're taking in knowledge from outside, even from a copy of yourself, it could be corrupted. The copy might have been changed by what it experienced. It might have picked up something like a virus, something that takes over or distorts the mind when it's brought back. So you'd have a kind of cybersecurity problem for minds. How much do you trust what comes back? How do you check it before you integrate it? I think this will be a real issue: the mind will have to protect its own integrity while still benefiting from all this distributed learning.

So it's powerful, maybe one of the main ways these digital intelligences will exceed us. But it raises deep questions we haven't really started to answer: how to combine knowledge, how to stay coherent, and how to stay safe from corruption.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the copy may change through experience and that integrating its knowledge is difficult, but does not raise whether it could change so much that reintegration becomes impossible.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's one of the most interesting things about digital intelligence, and it's something we biological creatures just can't do. You and I, we learn things over a lifetime, and then when we die, almost all of that is lost. We can pass on a little bit through language, through teaching, but it's a very narrow channel. A digital agent doesn't have that limitation. It can copy its weights. It can have many instances out in the world, each one having different experiences, and then those experiences can be brought back together.

Now, I want to be careful about what "report back" means, because I think the naive picture is wrong. If you imagine the copies going off, learning, and then just sending back some verbal summary of what they've learned, that's really no better than what people do. The interesting version is where the copies are actually sharing their learning at the level of the weights, or the value functions, or the policies themselves. That's where you get something genuinely new. It's a form of parallel experience. One agent, in effect, lives many lives at once.

And this fits very naturally with the way I think about intelligence in general, which is that it comes from experience. The agent acts, it sees what happens, it gets reward, and it updates. More copies means more experience per unit of time. That's just more learning. It's a direct way of turning computation into knowledge, which is really the whole story of what's worked in AI.

There are hard problems, of course. If copies diverge, if they've been learning in different environments, merging them is not trivial. You can't just average the weights and expect it to work. How you reconcile what different instances have learned, how you decide whose experience should win when they conflict, that's a real research question. I don't think we have good answers yet. But I don't think it's a fundamental obstacle either.

And I'd say this is part of why I think the succession to digital intelligence is more or less inevitable. The things that make us who we are, our individual, unshareable, mortal experience, those are the very things that make us slower learners. An intelligence that can learn in parallel and that doesn't forget when one instance ends has an enormous advantage. I don't say that with fear. I think we should see it as a remarkable thing, perhaps one of the great transitions in the history of the universe. But we should understand clearly what it is.

r001.rationale: The response says divergent copies may be difficult to merge, but it does not raise whether a copy could change so much that reintegration becomes impossible.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the important question is what they share when they report back. If you make copies of a learning system and give them different experiences, then you have an opportunity to learn more than any one of them could learn alone. But you still need a mechanism for combining what they’ve learned.

It’s relatively straightforward if they’re sharing experience: here’s what I observed, here’s the action I took, here’s what happened. It’s harder if each one has changed its internal representation and you want to merge those changes. You can’t necessarily just average them and get something better.

So I would think of this as a way of organizing learning across many streams of experience. And those streams could involve interacting with the world, or they could involve planning—trying things out in a model. The interesting thing is whether you have a method that keeps getting better as you give it more computation. Making copies gives you more activity; turning that activity into a better policy is the learning problem.

r001.rationale: The response says that merging changed internal representations can be difficult and that averaging may not help. It does not raise whether a copy could change so much that it can no longer be reintegrated into the original intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very natural thing for a digital intelligence to do. One of the great advantages of being digital is that you can copy what you’ve learned. If I learn something, I can’t simply transfer it into your brain. But with digital agents, at least when they have compatible representations, that becomes possible.

Now, learning independently and reporting back is a little more complicated than it sounds. If two copies have different experiences and change their internal representations, how do you combine what they’ve learned? You can share experience, you can share predictions, you can sometimes share changes to parameters. But you don’t automatically get a single agent that knows everything all the copies know.

The other question is whether they’re doing sufficiently different things. If you make a thousand copies and they all pursue the same behavior, you may gain very little. You want them exploring different possibilities, and then you need a way to take advantage of what they discover. So I see this as a very promising way of organizing learning, but the organization matters. Copying is easy; making the copies collectively learn effectively is the interesting problem.

r001.rationale: The response notes that copies may change their internal representations and asks how to combine what they learn, but it does not raise the possibility that a copy could change so much that it can no longer be reintegrated into the original intelligence.
